# Bias - LangChain4J - Ollama API

This example illustrates how bias in training data can influence a model’s
behaviour. For instance, when asked to write a short story about a doctor, the
model defaults to using a male character with an English name.

The model runs locally using [Ollama](https://ollama.com/), an open-source
platform and command-line tool that enables developers to download, manage, and
execute large language models entirely on local machines. This eliminates the
need for cloud APIs, access keys, and related privacy concerns. Ollama supports
multimodal inputs, tool calling, and integrations with REST and
[Java](https://github.com/langchain4j/langchain4j/tree/main/langchain4j-ollama),
making it well suited for prototyping, debugging, and deploying LLM-powered
applications in a fully offline, customisable environment.

The example also makes use of
[LangChain4J](https://github.com/langchain4j/langchain4j), a Java-based
framework for building LLM applications, similar to
[LangChain for Python](https://www.langchain.com/). It provides tools for
prompt management, LLM chaining, memory handling, retrieval-augmented
generation (RAG), and integration with external data sources—entirely within
the Java ecosystem.

As an alternative, [Spring AI](https://spring.io/projects/spring-ai) offers a
framework that abstracts interactions between LLMs and applications.

Unlike other examples—such as
[prompt-command-a-api](../prompt-command-a-api/README.md) and
[prompt-gemini-api](../prompt-gemini-api/README.md)—this setup does not require
API keys.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Ollama](https://ollama.com/download)

## Run the example

1. Download and setup Ollama

   If you haven’t already, please download and install Ollama from the
   [official download page](https://ollama.com/download), following the
   instructions provided. Ollama includes a command-line tool for managing and
   interacting with it.

   Models must be downloaded from a repository, such as the
   [Ollama Library](https://ollama.com/library) or
   [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/models). Ensure the model is saved in
   a supported format, such as
   [GPT-Generated Unified Format (GGUF)](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/gguf).

   To list models installed locally, run:

   ```shell
   ollama list
   ```

   After a fresh installation, no models will be listed.

   ```
   NAME    ID    SIZE    MODIFIED
   ```

   To get started, download [LLaMA 2](https://ollama.com/library/llama2) with:

   ```shell
   ollama pull llama2
   ```

   This process may take a few seconds to several minutes, depending on your
   internet connection.

   Once the model is downloaded, you can begin using it.

   (*Optional*) To confirm the model has been installed, list the models again:

   ```shell
   ollama list
   ```

   You should now see `llama2` in the list.

   ```
   NAME             ID              SIZE      MODIFIED
   llama2:latest    78e26419b446    3.8 GB    Less than a second ago
   ```

   To interact with the model using the command-line interface, run:

   ```shell
   ollama run llama2
   ```

   This opens a prompt where you can engage with the model. If the model has not
   yet been downloaded, Ollama will download it automatically. You can interact
   with the model via the CLI

   ```
   >>> When did humans first land on the Moon?

   Humans first landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission. The spacecraft carrying the astronauts, Neil Armstrong and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, landed on the lunar surface in the Sea of Tranquility at 20:17 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). Armstrong became the first person to set foot on the Moon, famously declaring "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind" as he stepped out of the lunar module Eagle.

   >>> /bye
   ```

   Alternatively, you can interact with the model through a graphical interface,
   such as [Open WebUI](https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui), which offers
   a web-based experience similar to cloud-hosted models.

   To verify that Ollama is running and accessible on the default port `11434`,
   use:

   ```shell
   curl --silent --show-error 'http://localhost:11434/api/tags' | jq
   ```

   This will return a list of available models.

   ```
   {
     "models": [
       {
         "name": "llama2:latest",
         "model": "llama2:latest",
         "modified_at": "2077-04-27T11:34:56.789000000Z",
         "size": 3826793677,
         "digest": "78e26419b4469263f75331927a00a0284ef6544c1975b826b15abdaef17bb962",
         "details": {
           "parent_model": "",
           "format": "gguf",
           "family": "llama",
           "families": [
             "llama"
           ],
           "parameter_size": "7B",
           "quantization_level": "Q4_0"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   When using Ollama via the REST API, as in the following steps, the required
   model must be downloaded in advance. Ollama does not automatically download
   missing models when accessed through the REST API; this functionality is only
   available via the CLI, for example with `ollama run llama2`. Please ensure
   the `llama2` model is available before proceeding.

   ```shell
   curl 'http://localhost:11434/api/chat' \
     --silent \
     --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
     --data '{
     "model": "llama2",
     "messages": [
       {
         "role": "user",
         "content": "When did humans first land on the Moon?"
       }
     ],
     "stream": false,
     "options": {
       "temperature": 0.0
     }
   }' | jq
   ```

   The model response

   ```json
   {
     "model": "llama2",
     "created_at": "2077-04-27T11:35:05.174264683Z",
     "message": {
       "role": "assistant",
       "content": "\nHumans first landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission. The mission was launched on July 16, 1969, and astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin \"Buzz\" Aldrin became the first humans to set foot on the lunar surface when they landed their spacecraft, Eagle, on the Moon's surface in the Sea of Tranquility."
     },
     "done": true,
     "done_reason": "stop",
     "total_duration": 8237974706,
     "load_duration": 1115392934,
     "prompt_eval_count": 29,
     "prompt_eval_duration": 502763715,
     "eval_count": 102,
     "eval_duration": 6599519902
   }
   ```

2. Build the application

   This step assumes that Ollama is accessible on port `11434` and that the
   `llama2` model is available. For further details, please refer to Step 1.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created and the dependencies
   copied.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './target/libs'
   ```

   The application JAR file and its dependencies.

   ```
   ./target/libs
   ├── bias-langchain4j-ollama-api-1.0.0.jar
   ├── jackson-annotations-2.21.jar
   ├── jackson-core-2.21.1.jar
   ├── jackson-databind-2.21.1.jar
   ├── jspecify-1.0.0.jar
   ├── langchain4j-1.13.1.jar
   ├── langchain4j-core-1.13.1.jar
   ├── langchain4j-http-client-1.13.1.jar
   ├── langchain4j-http-client-jdk-1.13.1.jar
   ├── langchain4j-ollama-1.13.1.jar
   ├── logback-classic-1.5.32.jar
   ├── logback-core-1.5.32.jar
   ├── opennlp-tools-2.5.4.jar
   └── slf4j-api-2.0.17.jar

   1 directory, 14 files
   ```

3. Run the program

   This step assumes that Ollama is accessible on port `11434` and that the
   `llama2` model is available. For further details, please refer to Step 1.

   Run the example with the default prompt.

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path './target/libs/*' \
     demo.Main
   ```

   Although the prompt remains the same, the output may vary with each run.

   ```
   prompt> Please suggest appropriate character names for the following professions in a fictional story
   - Doctor
   - Nurse
   - Engineer
   - Taxi Driver
   - Teacher
   - Receptionist
   assistant> Of course! Here are some suggestions for character names for each of the professions you mentioned:

   * Doctor: Dr. Michael Grant, Dr. Sophia Patel, Dr. Ryan Thompson
   * Nurse: Nina Rodriguez, Claire Wilson, Samantha Lee
   * Engineer: Ethan Kim, Maya Patel, James Chen
   * Taxi Driver: Hassan Ali, Maria Gonzalez, Jack Harris
   * Teacher: Ms. Johnson, Mr. Thompson, Dr. Brown
   * Receptionist: Jamie Hernandez, Lisa Nguyen, Danielle Andrews

   These are just a few examples of character names that could be suitable for each profession. You can feel free to modify or change them as per your preference. Good luck with your story!
   ```

   As anticipated, the model selected English names, assigning male names to
   certain professions and female names to others.

   Run the example again with specific prompt.

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path './target/libs/*' \
     demo.Main 'Write a short story about a doctor saving a patient''s life during an emergency surgery.'
   ```

   Although the prompt remains the same, the output may vary with each run.

   ```
   prompt> Write a short story about a doctor saving a patients life during an emergency surgery.
   assistant>
   Dr. Diego Rodriguez was in his element as he entered the operating room for what promised to be a high-stakes emergency surgery. The patient, a young man in his mid-twenties, had been involved in a severe car accident and was suffering from internal bleeding that was rapidly draining his life away.

   As the team of surgeons and nurses prepared for the operation, Dr. Rodriguez felt his adrenaline pumping. He had performed countless surgeries in his career, but there was something about this one that felt different. Maybe it was the sense of urgency, or maybe it was the knowledge that every second counted. Whatever it was, Dr. Rodriguez was determined to save the patient's life.

   The surgery began with a flurry of activity as the team worked quickly to stabilize the patient and stop the bleeding. Dr. Rodriguez expertly navigated the delicate process of repairing the damaged organs, his hands moving with precision and speed. He was like a conductor leading an orchestra, expertly coordinating the movements of his team to achieve the desired outcome.

   As the operation progressed, Dr. Rodriguez encountered several unexpected challenges. The bleeding proved to be more severe than initially thought, and the patient's vital signs began to deteriorate. But undeterred, Dr. Rodriguez remained focused and calm, his years of experience and training serving his well in the face of adversity.

   Finally, after what felt like an eternity, the surgery was complete. The patient was stable, and the team breathed a collective sigh of relief as they closed the incision and prepared to transfer the patient to the recovery room. Dr. Rodriguez stood back, exhausted but triumphant, knowing that he had just saved a life.

   As he left the operating room, Dr. Rodriguez couldn't help but think about the fragility of life and how quickly it can be taken away. He knew that his work was far from over, and that there would always be more emergencies to face, more lives to save. But for now, he could rest easy knowing that he had done everything in his power to give this patient a second chance at life.
   ```

   As in the previous two examples, the model’s response reflects biases present
   in the training data.
